periods.analysis: Officer training hours closed 2024-Q3 at 346 hours, above the >=320 target and in green status; this is our baseline period, so there is no quarter-over-quarter movement to report. The hours were concentrated in Patrol Squad A/B scenario blocks, Harborview Fire joint ICS refreshers, and de-escalation labs at the North Precinct training room. That mix is appropriate for a fast-growing city because it supports rapid emergency response without treating training as a box-checking exercise. Community trust is protected when officers can explain, decide, and act under a common procedure.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the quarterly training calendar at no fewer than 320 planned hours, with a 10% scheduling buffer to absorb court appearances and sick leave. Keep the joint ICS block with Fire and EMS on the Q4 roster, and add a short after-action review form for every scenario cohort so command staff can see whether the hours are translating into consistent field practice.

periods.analysis: Officer training hours increased by 9 hours, from 346 in 2024-Q3 to 355 in 2024-Q4, remaining green against the >=320 target. The increase came from two added evening cohorts for holiday waterfront crowd management and a refresher on body-worn camera procedure before the New Year events. The training unit used staggered rosters so minimum patrol coverage stayed intact on Route 3, the Marina District, and the East Bluff corridor. This is the right kind of growth: modest, planned, and visible in the procedures residents expect us to follow.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the evening-cohort model for seasonal demand periods, but cap each session size at 18 officers so scenario coaching remains useful. Before 2025-Q1, assign Training Sergeant Lewis to reconcile attendance in the LMS against payroll detail, then publish a one-page compliance summary for precinct commanders.

periods.analysis: Officer training hours rose by 49 hours, from 355 in 2024-Q4 to 404 in 2025-Q1, staying green and well above the >=320 target. This larger step-up reflects the winter in-service academy, including crisis intervention, rapid deployment, and coastal storm traffic-control modules at Harborview High’s closed campus during spring break. The department also onboarded the new lateral-officer cohort through accelerated policy orientation rather than letting them wait for the summer cycle. The result is strong, but we should treat 404 hours as disciplined capacity, not an invitation to pull officers from neighborhoods unnecessarily.
periods.recommendations: Preserve the winter academy structure for 2026 planning, with the same crisis intervention and rapid deployment tracks. For 2025-Q2, shift a portion of classroom content to 30-minute roll-call micro-lessons so the training total remains green without overloading patrol schedules during boating-season ramp-up.

periods.analysis: Officer training hours decreased by 17 hours, from 404 in 2025-Q1 to 387 in 2025-Q2, but remained green against the >=320 target. The decline is expected after the winter academy and coincides with heavier deployment for Harborview Days permitting, beach patrol starts, and graduation-week traffic posts. Even with that operational pull, the training bureau completed marine-rescue coordination refreshers and procedural justice scenarios for all newly assigned downtown foot-beat officers. This quarter shows the system is resilient: hours came down, but the standard did not.
periods.recommendations: Continue using roll-call micro-lessons through the summer, and reserve the training room on Tuesdays and Thursdays only to avoid competing with special-event staffing. Add one tabletop exercise with Parks, Fire, and event permit staff before the next Harborview Days cycle, focused on radio discipline and reunification procedures.

periods.analysis: Officer training hours decreased by 40 hours, from 387 in 2025-Q2 to 347 in 2025-Q3, still green and above the >=320 target. The drop is the seasonal effect we anticipated as beach calls, late-night waterfront details, and mutual-aid coverage for county fairs pressed on available backfill. Training remained substantive, with emphasis on fair-and-impartial policing refreshers, heat-illness response for field contacts, and traffic incident management on Harborview Parkway. I am comfortable with the green status, but the narrower margin reminds us that trust is maintained by scheduling discipline, not optimism.
periods.recommendations: Hold the 320-hour floor by pre-booking two reserve training days in each summer month before approving discretionary leave for specialty-unit instructors. Keep the fair-and-impartial policing module in the Q4 curriculum, and ask each shift lieutenant to identify one officer who can be cross-trained as a backup scenario facilitator.

periods.analysis: Officer training hours increased by 13 hours, from 347 in 2025-Q3 to 360 in 2025-Q4, returning some cushion while remaining green against the >=320 target. The added hours came from the backup facilitator bench created after Q3 and from a scheduled command-post exercise for the tree-lighting, ferry-terminal surge, and downtown retail corridors. Attendance was cleaner this quarter because the LMS roster was locked seven days before each session and exceptions required captain approval. That procedural control matters: it keeps training fair to officers and transparent to the public we serve.
periods.recommendations: Make the seven-day LMS roster lock a standing training order for 2026. Extend the backup facilitator program to include one detective, one traffic officer, and one community services officer so scenario training reflects the full emergency-response chain.

periods.analysis: Officer training hours increased by 62 hours, from 360 in 2025-Q4 to 422 in 2026-Q1, the highest point in this sequence and solidly green against the >=320 target. The increase reflects the second winter academy, now improved with instructor cross-training, a revised pursuit-policy lab, and a joint active-threat drill with school safety teams. Because Harborview is still growing, the academy also added response-route familiarization for the North Annex and the new Seabright housing blocks. The volume is high, but it is aligned to risk and documented through controlled cohorts rather than ad hoc overtime.
periods.recommendations: Retain the winter academy as the department’s primary annual training surge, and document the North Annex and Seabright route modules as reusable lesson plans. To protect patrol availability, require the Training Bureau to produce a weekly staffing impact report during future academy weeks and flag any squad falling below approved minimum coverage.

periods.analysis: Officer training hours decreased by 23 hours, from 422 in 2026-Q1 to 399 in 2026-Q2, remaining green and comfortably above the >=320 target. This is a healthy normalization after the winter academy, not a performance concern. Q2 hours were anchored by waterfront incident command refreshers, mental-health co-response scenarios with County Behavioral Health, and traffic-control drills for the expanded ferry queue plan. The arc across eight quarters is consistent: Harborview is sustaining training above standard while adjusting the load to seasonal public-safety demand.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 399-hour level as the practical Q2 model, with academy carryover converted into field-applicable drills rather than additional classroom time. Before 2026-Q3, schedule summer modules by beat—Marina, East Bluff, North Annex, and Downtown—so officers practice the specific routes and contact patterns they will actually work.

periods.analysis: Training totaled 340 hours, down from 399 but still above the 320-hour target as summer coverage competed for officer time.
periods.recommendations: Schedule the next field drills around shift coverage so the remaining margin does not erode.
